name: Barossa Valley
description: Shiraz from vines older than most wine countries' industries: dense, sweet-fruited and chocolatey, from ungrafted bush vines planted in the 1840s.
funFact: Australia never suffered phylloxera in South Australia, so the Barossa holds some of the oldest continuously producing vines on earth — several plantings date to the 1840s and are still cropped.

serve.how: Serve a few degrees below room temperature; at 68°F and above the alcohol and sweetness take over completely. Decant young bottles for an hour. The old-vine wines carry their weight better than the alcohol suggests, so judge them on texture rather than on the number on the label.

composition.summary: Old-vine Shiraz from a warm, dry valley on ungrafted, dry-farmed bush vines.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Shiraz, with Grenache and Mataro alongside.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Barossa Valley in South Australia, warm and largely dry-farmed.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Warm fermentation with generous extraction; some open-fermenter work.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–24 months in American and French oak.

composition.process: Hot, dry ripening on very old low-yielding vines concentrates the fruit, and extended oak ageing rounds the tannin into the region's signature plushness.

name: Hunter Valley
description: The world's most unlikely great white: Semillon picked early at ten percent alcohol, unoaked and searingly tart young, which transforms into toast and honey after a decade.
funFact: Hunter Semillon is bottled young at around 10.5% with no oak at all, yet develops toasty, honeyed complexity over ten to twenty years — one of the few wines that gains oak-like character without ever seeing a barrel.

serve.how: A young bottle is austere and lemony and genuinely hard work — the style is designed for age, so if you have one under five years old, consider keeping it. An aged bottle should be served slightly warmer, around 52°F, so the toast and beeswax come through. Neither version needs decanting.

composition.summary: Early-picked, unoaked Semillon built for long bottle development.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Semillon.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Lower Hunter Valley of New South Wales, humid and subtropical.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Picked early at low sugar, cool stainless fermentation, bottled young.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: No oak whatsoever; all complexity develops in bottle.

composition.process: Early picking retains very high acidity at low alcohol, and long reductive bottle ageing converts the primary citrus into toast and honey without any barrel contact.

name: Coonawarra
description: A nine-mile strip of red terra rossa soil over limestone, producing Cabernet with mint, cassis and a firm line of acidity found nowhere else in Australia.
funFact: The famous terra rossa strip is barely nine miles long and one mile wide, and boundary disputes over which vineyards fall inside it have gone through Australian courts.

serve.how: Decant a young bottle for an hour to soften the firm tannin structure. Serve cool in a large glass. The eucalypt-mint note is a regional marker rather than a flaw; it integrates with age, and these wines hold well for fifteen years or more thanks to their acidity.

composition.summary: Cabernet Sauvignon on a narrow band of terra rossa soil over limestone.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Cabernet Sauvignon, with some Shiraz and Merlot.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The terra rossa strip of Coonawarra in South Australia's cool Limestone Coast.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Destemmed, fermented with moderate extraction to keep the structure fine.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–18 months in French oak.

composition.process: Cool ripening on free-draining terra rossa over limestone gives cassis fruit with firm acidity and fine tannin, structured for long ageing.

name: Margaret River
description: Maritime Western Australia making Bordeaux blends of unusual polish, alongside some of the country's finest Chardonnay — a region only planted since 1967.
funFact: Margaret River was planted on the strength of a 1965 agronomy paper arguing its climate matched Bordeaux — one of the few wine regions founded on a scientific prediction rather than tradition.

serve.how: Serve cool in a large glass and decant young reds for around forty minutes. These are structured but not heavy; the maritime climate gives a freshness that separates them from warmer Australian regions. The Chardonnay from here deserves the same care and should be served at white-wine temperature.

composition.summary: Maritime Bordeaux blends and Chardonnay from a peninsula between two oceans.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, with Chardonnay and Sauvignon-Semillon for whites.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Margaret River peninsula in Western Australia, surrounded by ocean on three sides.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Careful extraction, with barrel fermentation for the whites.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–18 months in French oak.

composition.process: A strongly maritime climate with almost no extreme heat gives even ripening and natural freshness, producing wines with structure but without the weight of inland Australia.

name: Yarra Valley
description: Cool-climate Victoria, close enough to Melbourne to be its wine country: fine traditional-method sparkling and delicate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
funFact: Moët & Chandon established Domaine Chandon here in 1986, choosing the Yarra over every other Australian region for sparkling wine on the basis of its cool nights and long, slow ripening.

serve.how: Serve well chilled in a tulip rather than a flute so the brioche and almond notes have room. Pour gently at an angle. These are made in the traditional method with genuine lees ageing, so give them the attention you would give Champagne rather than treating them as a cheap alternative.

composition.summary: Cool-climate traditional-method sparkling wine from Victoria's Yarra Valley.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, with some Pinot Meunier.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Yarra Valley east of Melbourne, cool and often cloudy.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Traditional method with secondary fermentation in bottle.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 18–36 months on lees before disgorgement.

composition.process: Cool ripening keeps acidity high and sugar low at harvest, which is exactly the base wine that traditional-method secondary fermentation requires.

name: Clare Valley
description: Australia's Riesling heartland: bone dry, lime-drenched and steely, sealed under screwcap since 2000 when the region switched almost overnight.
funFact: Clare Valley producers collectively moved to screwcap in 2000 to stop cork taint ruining their Riesling — a coordinated regional decision that pushed the whole Australian industry to follow.

serve.how: Serve well chilled in a standard white glass. Young Clare Riesling is austere and citric; with five to ten years it develops a toasty, kerosene-like complexity that is prized rather than faulty. Do not decant. Screwcap closures mean these age slowly and reliably, so cellaring is genuinely rewarding.

composition.summary: Bone-dry, high-acid Riesling from a warm region with very cold nights.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Riesling.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Clare Valley in South Australia, elevated with cold night-time temperatures.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool stainless-steel fermentation, fermented fully dry.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: No oak; bottled young under screwcap.

composition.process: Warm days with sharply cold nights hold acidity while ripening the fruit, and a fully dry stainless fermentation leaves the lime and mineral character exposed.

name: McLaren Vale
description: Maritime Shiraz and Grenache south of Adelaide: darker and more savoury than the Barossa, with a growing body of dry-grown old-vine Grenache.
funFact: McLaren Vale sits close enough to the Gulf St Vincent for afternoon sea breezes to drop vineyard temperatures sharply, which is why its Shiraz reads savoury where the Barossa's reads sweet.

serve.how: Serve cool in a large glass. Decant young Shiraz for half an hour; the old-vine Grenache generally needs less and can be served slightly cooler still. The savoury, olive-and-herb character is the regional signature and is easily lost if the wine is served warm.

composition.summary: Maritime-cooled Shiraz and old-vine Grenache on varied ancient soils.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Shiraz and Grenache, with Mataro and Cabernet Sauvignon.

components.label: Region
components.detail: McLaren Vale south of Adelaide, cooled by gulf breezes.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Warm fermentation, increasingly with whole bunches for the Grenache.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–18 months in French oak, often seasoned rather than new.

composition.process: Sea breezes moderate an otherwise warm climate, preserving acidity and giving savoury notes that distinguish it from inland South Australian reds.

name: Rutherglen
description: Fortified Muscat aged for decades in hot tin sheds until it turns to treacle, raisin and burnt orange. Some blends contain wine over a century old.
funFact: The classification runs Rutherglen, Classic, Grand and Rare, with average blend ages rising to twenty years and beyond — and the solera-style blends often include material from the nineteenth century.

serve.how: Serve in small measures, barely cool or at room temperature — chilling mutes the whole point. It is intensely sweet and viscous, so an ounce or two is plenty. An open bottle keeps for months rather than days thanks to the fortification and oxidative ageing, so there is no rush to finish it.

composition.summary: Fortified Muscat aged oxidatively in hot conditions for years to decades.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Muscat à Petits Grains Rouges, known locally as Brown Muscat.

components.label: Region
components.detail: Rutherglen in north-east Victoria, hot and continental.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Grapes left to raisin on the vine, then fortified with grape spirit mid-fermentation.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Years to decades in old oak in hot sheds, blended solera-style.

composition.process: Fermentation is arrested by fortification to retain enormous sugar, and deliberate hot oxidative ageing concentrates the wine into its treacle-and-raisin character.

name: Marlborough
description: The Sauvignon Blanc that rewrote the grape's reputation: passionfruit, cut grass and grapefruit at a pitch no other region reaches.
funFact: The first Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc was made in 1979, and within twenty years the style was so dominant that it changed what consumers worldwide expected the grape to taste like.

serve.how: Serve well chilled in a standard white glass — over-chilling flattens the aromatics that are the entire proposition. Drink it young; the pyrazine and thiol compounds responsible for the passionfruit and grass fade within two or three years. No decanting, and no need for a large bowl.

composition.summary: Intensely aromatic Sauvignon Blanc from a sunny, cool valley on free-draining gravels.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Sauvignon Blanc.

components.label: Region
components.detail: The Wairau and Awatere valleys of Marlborough, sunny with very cool nights.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool stainless fermentation under reductive conditions to protect thiols.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: No oak; bottled young.

composition.process: High sunshine with cold nights builds aromatic precursors while holding acidity, and reductive cool fermentation preserves the thiol compounds that give the passionfruit character.

name: Central Otago
description: The world's southernmost wine region: Pinot Noir grown in a continental mountain basin, dark-fruited and thyme-scented with real structure.
funFact: Central Otago is the only genuinely continental wine climate in New Zealand — everywhere else is maritime — which is why its Pinot Noir is darker and firmer than the country's other examples.

serve.how: Serve at cellar temperature in a wide Burgundy bowl. These are more structured than most New World Pinot and benefit from thirty minutes open, though not from aggressive decanting. The wild thyme note is a regional marker and shows best when the wine is not over-warmed.

composition.summary: Continental-climate Pinot Noir from steep schist slopes in a mountain basin.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Pinot Noir.

components.label: Region
components.detail: Central Otago in the South Island interior, at 45 degrees south.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Partial whole-cluster fermentation, moderate extraction.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 10–18 months in French oak, a small proportion new.

composition.process: A dry continental climate with intense sunlight and cold nights ripens Pinot Noir fully while retaining acidity, giving darker fruit and firmer tannin than maritime sites.

name: Hawke's Bay
description: New Zealand's warmest major region and its answer to Bordeaux: Merlot and Cabernet blends grown on the old riverbed gravels of the Gimblett district.
funFact: The Gimblett Gravels sub-region is defined by an old riverbed exposed when the Ngaruroro River shifted course in an 1867 flood — the appellation boundary follows the gravel exactly.

serve.how: Serve cool in a large glass and decant young bottles briefly. These are medium-bodied rather than heavy, so avoid treating them like a warm-climate Cabernet. The Syrah from the same gravels is peppery and floral and deserves slightly cooler service still.

composition.summary: Bordeaux varieties and Syrah on free-draining river gravels in New Zealand's warmest region.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Syrah.

components.label: Region
components.detail: Hawke's Bay on the North Island's east coast, including the Gimblett Gravels.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Destemmed and fermented with moderate extraction.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–18 months in French oak.

composition.process: Heat-retaining river gravels raise vineyard temperatures enough to ripen Bordeaux varieties in a cool maritime country, giving medium-bodied and cedary wines.

name: Martinborough
description: A tiny North Island region on a windswept gravel terrace, making Pinot Noir of unusual savoury intensity from very low-yielding vines.
funFact: Martinborough's persistent wind is a viticultural asset rather than a hazard — it thickens grape skins and cuts yields sharply, which concentrates the resulting wines.

serve.how: Serve at cellar temperature in a wide bowl. These are savoury, structured Pinots rather than fruit-forward ones, and they show best with twenty minutes of air. They also age well for a New World Pinot, so a bottle with five years on it is often more expressive than a current release.

composition.summary: Low-yielding, savoury Pinot Noir from a wind-exposed gravel terrace.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Pinot Noir.

components.label: Region
components.detail: Martinborough in the Wairarapa, on a free-draining alluvial terrace.

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Whole-cluster inclusion common, with careful extraction.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 12–18 months in French oak, mostly used.

composition.process: Constant wind and free-draining gravel reduce yields dramatically, concentrating flavour, while whole-cluster fermentation adds the savoury spice the region is known for.
